## Limitations and Open Problems

The open-problems discussion here follows the review's existing organizing choice: limitations are grouped by whether they arise from the foundational NeRF representation, the differentiable volume-rendering computation, the static per-scene learning setup, or extensions needed for scale and deployment. These are source-supported trade-offs of the cited methods, not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering research. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8]

The first foundational limitation is computational. Rendering a pixel requires casting a ray and evaluating the neural network at many 3D sample positions to approximate the volume-rendering integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as requiring hundreds of network evaluations per pixel and identify repeated ray marching through a large MLP as the barrier to real-time or interactive rendering. This cost affects both optimization and novel-view generation: the same differentiable integration that enables supervision from posed images also makes training and inference sample intensive. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:4baacae88add] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:ed5c2ff4a7e2] Hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling mitigates but does not remove this cost. It allocates more samples to regions expected to contribute to the image by converting coarse compositing weights into a depth distribution and drawing additional fine samples from it. The method therefore improves sample placement relative to uniform or stratified evaluation, but the fine renderer still evaluates a network at the union of coarse and second-stage samples. It is an importance-like allocation strategy within volume rendering, not a constant-time representation or a replacement for ray integration. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f]

A second limitation is that the continuous MLP representation is not automatically efficient to deploy on conventional graphics hardware. Baked sparse voxel grids can accelerate rendering, but the SNeRG description notes that such grids still require ray marching and substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF instead moves to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization with a small fragment-shader MLP, while DNMP uses deformable mesh primitives to obtain rasterization efficiency. These systems illustrate a trade-off: preserving the original continuous volumetric field is convenient for differentiable view synthesis, whereas interactive hardware deployment often motivates changing the data structure and rendering path. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:ef5225226b22]

The base representation also does not provide an explicit, readily editable surface. NeRF stores density and view-dependent radiance as a continuous function queried along rays, rather than a triangle mesh or another explicit geometry object. Later work notes that NeRF-style fields can have high rendering quality but structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation. This does not mean surfaces cannot be extracted from some NeRF variants; rather, explicit editing, mesh export, and physical geometry tasks are not directly supplied by the foundational density-and-radiance MLP. [E:arxiv:2507.11971:abstract:claim:2730a1af752f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] View-dependent radiance creates a related geometry-appearance ambiguity. Although density is nominally a function of 3D position and color is a function of position and direction, the network can explain some image changes using view-dependent color rather than uniquely correct geometry. Work on the shape-radiance ambiguity analyzes this possibility, and VDN-NeRF states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting. Its response is to normalize or distill view-dependent information so geometry is less affected, without changing the volume-rendering pipeline; this confirms that simply adding c(x,d) does not disentangle shape, material, illumination, and motion. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:cc17a11de600] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:19e1b65754b8] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02]

The original emitted-radiance model also has limited physical scope. It can represent direction-dependent color such as simple specular appearance, but it does not explicitly trace reflection rays or decompose outgoing radiance into materials and lighting. Surface-based inverse-rendering systems can recover meshes, materials, and lighting, but the MobileNeRF excerpt notes a significant loss in view-synthesis quality for that class of approach and difficulty with expensive global illumination on mobile hardware. Conversely, later reflection-aware NeRF work adds traced reflection rays because expensive direct neural radiance queries and consistent nearby reflections remain difficult. These are extensions beyond the original c(x,d) parameterization. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:62a1e5ae8a8d]

Multiscale viewing is another unresolved property of the original point-ray formulation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and point-like 5D coordinates. Mip-NeRF reports that this can yield blur or aliasing when training and testing images observe content at different scales; simply casting more rays is expensive because every extra ray multiplies MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical frustums and integrated positional encoding reduce aliasing in that paper, while Mip-VoG later pursues explicit multiscale grids for real-time anti-aliasing. Thus, the foundational renderer integrates a ray but does not itself prefilter the spatial footprint of a pixel. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:134e66531564] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:8cf251239f23] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:644db93cbf81] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:5bad30e8f677]

The learning setting is restrictive as well. Foundational NeRF optimizes a separate network for each scene from posed images. PixelNeRF identifies two consequences of this regime: many calibrated views and significant optimization time are required for the original scene-specific approach. Its image-conditioned, cross-scene architecture is designed to predict a scene representation from one or few views, but that is a different feed-forward learning problem with its own generalization and uncertainty challenges. Therefore, sparse-view or single-image reconstruction should not be treated as solved by the original per-scene optimization. [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:8181648b99c2] The static-scene assumption is also part of the foundational boundary. The original 5D field contains position and viewing direction but no time or deformation coordinate. HyperNeRF motivates its higher-dimensional model by explaining that deformation-based dynamic NeRFs use continuous mappings into a canonical space and therefore struggle with topological changes, which require discontinuity. HyperNeRF's per-image slices through a higher-dimensional field target dynamic interpolation and fixed-moment novel-view synthesis, indicating that changing topology and non-rigid motion are outside the base static formulation. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:5ccb35148c9e] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53]

Finally, architectural acceleration introduces its own trade-offs rather than a single universal solution. PVD describes plain MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and their compositions as competing NeRF structures with distinct trade-offs; it specifically notes that hash-table representations train and render faster but lack clear geometric meaning for spatial-relation-aware editing. Hyb-NeRF similarly combines encodings to balance speed, quality, aliasing, and memory. The open problem is therefore not merely making NeRF faster: practitioners must jointly choose representation interpretability, storage, rendering hardware, multiscale behavior, editability, and view-synthesis fidelity. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6b2c3eff679] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:c317f01e8195] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:section:abstract:1:80a6a4758916:claim:2e11b9886350]

## Conclusion

The core answer is therefore a continuous per-scene neural radiance field coupled to a transmittance-weighted ray integral. Density supplies opacity-like termination probability, while direction-conditioned radiance permits non-Lambertian appearance; the discrete renderer turns sampled density and color into a differentiable pixel prediction. The main trade-off is that this formulation enables photometric optimization and 3D-consistent view synthesis, but requires many network evaluations along rays, uses a static scene-specific model, and does not by itself provide explicit surfaces, material–lighting decomposition, or multiscale prefiltering. input.query: Explain the foundational NeRF representation and differentiable volume-rendering formulation.
input.survey:
# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Radiance Field Learned Through Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF addresses static novel-view synthesis by optimizing, for each scene, a fully connected MLP that maps a continuous 5D coordinate—3D position plus viewing direction—to position-dependent volume density and view-dependent RGB radiance. Camera rays are sampled in 3D, and pixel color is formed by differentiable alpha compositing: each interval contributes its color weighted by alpha and accumulated transmittance. This makes density and color trainable from posed images without explicit 3D supervision. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are the original refinements that support high-frequency detail and allocate samples toward visible content. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:cab0b40a18e0] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:e3e4173a53ad] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f]

## Introduction

This review is organized around the two foundational components requested by the question: first, the neural scene representation—what coordinates NeRF consumes and what physical quantities it predicts—and second, the differentiable rendering model that turns those field samples into pixel colors and training gradients. This grouping is an explanatory choice for the foundational method, not a universal taxonomy of later NeRF variants. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02]

The problem addressed by the original NeRF is novel-view synthesis from a sparse set of observed images with known camera poses. Rather than explicitly reconstructing a mesh or storing a discrete voxel grid, NeRF optimizes a continuous volumetric scene function for each scene using a fully connected, non-convolutional network. The network maps a single continuous 5D coordinate—three spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and two viewing-direction coordinates (θ, φ)—to volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:cab0b40a18e0]

The scope of the foundational representation is therefore a field over rays in 3D space: density is attached to a spatial location, while RGB radiance can vary with the direction from which that location is observed. This permits the model to describe non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights, while still using density to encode occupancy-like opacity. The learned field is queried at points sampled along camera rays; it is not, in the original formulation, a feed-forward predictor shared across scenes or conditioned directly on input images. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:e3e4173a53ad] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04]

Images are formed by classical volume rendering made differentiable. For a camera ray r(t)=o+td bounded by near and far distances, NeRF integrates the radiance c(r(t),d) weighted by density σ(r(t)) and accumulated transmittance T(t), where T(t)=exp(−∫σ(r(s))ds). Density acts as the differential probability that the ray terminates at a point, and transmittance is the probability that the ray reaches that point without earlier termination. Because the rendered color is a differentiable composite of network outputs, NeRF can be optimized from posed 2D images alone without explicit 3D supervision. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is to separate three questions that foundational NeRF combines: what is represented, how a representation is rendered into an image, and what the optimization target is. The representation criterion asks whether a method stores geometry and appearance in a continuous coordinate-based field, an explicit grid, polygons, mesh primitives, or another data structure. The rendering criterion asks whether pixel color is produced by differentiable volume integration, rasterization, ray tracing, or a hybrid shader. The supervision criterion asks whether training is per-scene optimization from posed images or feed-forward prediction conditioned on images. These are comparison dimensions, not a claim that later work falls into a fixed number of categories. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f] Foundational NeRF belongs at the intersection of continuous neural fields and differentiable volume rendering: its MLP is a per-scene 5D function from position and viewing direction to density and radiance, and its image formation model integrates samples along each ray. This differs from methods whose primary representation is an explicit textured polygon mesh or deformable mesh primitive. MobileNeRF, for example, uses polygons carrying binary-opacity textures and feature vectors, then relies on z-buffered rasterization and a small view-dependent fragment shader; DNMP parameterizes local geometry and radiance with connected deformable mesh vertices and vertex features. Those approaches may preserve NeRF-style view synthesis, but they do not use the original continuous MLP-plus-ray-integral representation as their core storage. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:ef5225226b22] A second distinction is between the field parameterization and the acceleration structure used to evaluate it. Later NeRF architectures may replace or augment a plain MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, tri-plane structures, voxel caches, or hybrid multi-resolution encodings; PVD explicitly treats MLP, sparse, low-rank, hash-table, and composite forms as convertible NeRF architectures with different trade-offs. Such variants can still be rendered by volume compositing, so changing the parameterization is not the same as replacing differentiable volume rendering. Conversely, a baked grid or polygon representation may be designed specifically to avoid repeated large-MLP evaluations during ray marching or to use standard GPU rasterization. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:1e1edc33ac5d] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6b2c3eff679] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] The foundational rendering relationship should also be distinguished from anti-aliasing and scale-aware extensions. Original NeRF casts one ray per pixel and queries point-like 5D coordinates along that ray. Mip-NeRF changes the sampling primitive from a ray to a conical frustum and uses integrated positional encoding so that a query represents the volume and scale covered by a pixel; Mip-VoG instead uses explicit multiscale voxel grids with level-of-detail selection and a deferred network for real-time anti-aliasing. These methods address aliasing across image scales, whereas the original volume-rendering equation is concerned with integrating density and radiance along a ray. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:134e66531564] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:8cf251239f23] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:644db93cbf81] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:5bad30e8f677] Task scope is another boundary. The original NeRF objective is static-scene novel-view synthesis: optimize one scene representation from images and known poses, then render new camera views. PixelNeRF remains compatible with NeRF's volume-rendering supervision but changes the learning setting by conditioning a network on one or few input images and learning a cross-scene prior. HyperNeRF instead targets dynamic or non-rigid scenes and models per-image radiance fields as slices through a higher-dimensional field, addressing a limitation of continuous deformation fields when topology changes. These are extensions in input conditioning or time/configuration modeling, not alternative statements of the original static 5D field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:5ccb35148c9e] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:8181648b99c2] Finally, differentiable volume rendering should not be equated with every differentiable-rendering objective. Surface-based inverse rendering can optimize meshes, occupancy, materials, and lighting through differentiable rasterization or marching-tetrahedra pipelines; some later mobile reconstruction systems combine explicit surfaces, implicit textures, and lightweight shaders. Those methods may be trained from images and produce view-dependent appearance, but their image-formation path and geometric assumptions differ from NeRF's transmittance-weighted volumetric integral. The foundational NeRF classification is therefore narrow but precise: a continuous, per-scene, position-and-direction-conditioned radiance field, rendered by differentiable density-weighted compositing along camera rays. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:ed5c2ff4a7e2]

## Representative Methods

The foundational NeRF mechanism is a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron optimized separately for one scene. Its learned function takes a 5D input consisting of spatial position x=(x,y,z) and viewing direction d, represented in the original paper through direction coordinates (θ,φ), and returns two kinds of quantities at that ray sample: a scalar volume density σ(x) and an emitted color c(x,d), typically RGB. The architectural split matters: density depends on position, whereas color depends on both position and viewing direction, allowing the same occupied location to have direction-dependent appearance. The original network is fully connected and non-convolutional; it is not a discrete mesh, voxel occupancy array, or image-to-3D predictor. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:e3e4173a53ad] This representation is continuous in the sense used by NeRF: the MLP can be queried at arbitrary continuous 3D coordinates along a ray, rather than only at cells of a fixed grid. The field is nevertheless optimized from finite posed images. Camera rays are generated for image pixels, sample coordinates are evaluated by the network, and the resulting density-color pairs are projected into pixel colors. The only geometric input required by the original optimization is the collection of training images with known camera poses; explicit 3D labels such as point clouds or surface meshes are not required for the core view-synthesis objective. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] The physical interpretation of the field is volumetric rather than strictly surface based. At position x, σ(x) is interpreted as the differential probability that a ray terminates on an infinitesimal particle there. High density therefore behaves like opaque or strongly participating matter, while low or zero density permits the ray to continue. Unlike a hard binary surface, this formulation can represent soft occupancy and semi-transparent content through continuous density. Color is emitted radiance conditioned on view direction, which is how the model captures view-varying effects such as specular appearance without explicitly decomposing the scene into material and lighting parameters. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53]

For rendering, a camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o, unit direction d, and near and far bounds t_n and t_f. NeRF defines the expected color of that ray as C(r)=∫_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d) dt. The term T(t)=exp(−∫_{t_n}^{t}σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: it gives the probability that the ray travels from the near bound to t without interacting earlier. The integrand therefore combines the probability of reaching a sample, the local probability of interacting there, and the radiance emitted back along the ray. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] The continuous integral is not evaluated analytically. NeRF estimates it numerically by querying the MLP at discrete samples along each ray. A common discrete rendering form uses sample colors c_i, densities σ_i, and interval widths δ_i. The alpha value for interval i is α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i), and transmittance is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j)=Π_{j<i}(1−α_j). The rendered ray color is then Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i. This is alpha compositing over depth-ordered volumetric samples; because every operation—sampling coordinates, MLP evaluation, exponentials, products, and weighted summation—is differentiable, image reconstruction loss can update the field weights. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] The original implementation uses stratified sampling for its initial set of ray samples. The near-to-far interval is divided into evenly spaced bins, and one sample is drawn uniformly from each bin. This deterministic stratification with within-bin randomness provides coverage across the ray while encouraging the network to learn a continuous representation rather than overfitting samples at exactly the same depths. These coarse samples are sufficient to define the basic renderer, but the original paper reports that the basic components alone do not reach its state-of-the-art quality; two refinements are introduced for high-resolution complex scenes. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd]

The first refinement is positional encoding. Raw low-dimensional coordinates are passed through high-frequency sinusoidal mappings before entering the MLP. NeRF introduces this mapping because deep networks on low-dimensional coordinates can be biased toward smoother functions; the lifted coordinates make high-frequency variation in geometry and appearance easier to optimize. In the original architecture, positional encoding is applied to both spatial coordinates and viewing-direction coordinates, although the encoding bandwidth and network use differ according to the roles of position and direction. This is a representation/input transformation, not a change to the volume-rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:e3e4173a53ad] The second refinement is hierarchical volume sampling, implemented with coarse and fine networks. The coarse network is first evaluated at N_c stratified samples. Its rendered color can be rewritten as Ĉ_c(r)=Σ_i w_i c_i with w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)). Normalizing these weights gives a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray depth. NeRF then draws N_f additional samples from that distribution by inverse transform sampling, evaluates the fine network at the union of original and second-stage locations, and renders the final color using all N_c+N_f samples. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] Hierarchical sampling changes where computation is spent, not the underlying compositing rule. Free space and occluded regions generally receive low coarse weights, whereas visible density receives higher weights, so the second stage places more fine samples near content expected to affect the image. The paper explicitly distinguishes this from treating each sample as an independent Monte Carlo estimate of the whole integral: the normalized coarse weights define a nonuniform discretization of the ray interval. The coarse rendering is still supervised, so the first network learns weights useful for allocating the second network's samples. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd]

Training follows the renderer. For a selected pixel, a ray is cast through the scene, field samples are rendered into a predicted RGB color, and that prediction is compared with the observed pixel color. In the coarse-to-fine system, the loss includes both the coarse and fine renderings; the original paper's objective is the sum of the coarse and fine mean-squared color errors over rays. Gradients propagate from the pixel loss through the discrete transmittance-weighted composition to the colors and densities predicted by the MLPs. Repeating this optimization over many posed views fits a single scene's continuous radiance field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] At inference, the same renderer is used for novel camera views. Given a new pose, NeRF casts rays through the desired image plane, samples the learned field, and composites each ray into a pixel color. The network does not need to retrieve a nearby training image or warp an observed view; novel views are generated by evaluating the learned 5D function and integrating it along rays. This is why the method is described as a 3D-consistent continuous volumetric scene function rather than an image-space interpolation scheme. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:cab0b40a18e0] The view-dependent branch has a specific scope: it explains appearance changes with observation direction while density remains a function of 3D location. This supports non-Lambertian effects such as highlights, but it does not by itself provide an explicit separation of geometry, reflectance, illumination, and shadows. Later work may normalize or distill view dependence to improve geometry under moving lights, add reflection rays for specular transport, or perform inverse rendering for materials and lighting. Those mechanisms address phenomena beyond the original NeRF assumption that emitted radiance can be represented directly as c(x,d). [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:19e1b65754b8] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:62a1e5ae8a8d] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d]

The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is also important. It models a static scene with a per-scene optimized MLP and known camera poses. PixelNeRF changes that learning regime by conditioning a NeRF on one or more input images and learning a prior across scenes, enabling feed-forward prediction from sparse views. HyperNeRF changes the static-scene assumption by addressing dynamic, non-rigid scenes and topology variation. Neither modification is required to explain the original representation, and neither should be conflated with the base method's single-scene static 5D field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:5ccb35148c9e] The original formulation also does not solve aliasing by construction. It casts a single ray per pixel and queries point locations; mip-NeRF later argues that this can produce blur or aliasing when content is observed at different resolutions and replaces point-ray queries with anti-aliased conical frustums and integrated positional encoding. Thus, the foundational volume-rendering equation explains how samples are integrated for a ray, while multiscale prefiltering is a separate extension. Mip-NeRF reports being about 7% faster than NeRF and half the size, with error reductions of 17% on the NeRF dataset and 60% on a multiscale variant, but those results characterize the extension rather than the base method's mechanism. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:134e66531564] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:8cf251239f23] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:712dfa864837] Computational cost follows directly from the base mechanism. Each pixel requires ray marching, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at sampled 3D locations to approximate the integral. Later acceleration work identifies this repeated network evaluation as the reason vanilla NeRF is expensive to train and render; proposed responses include hash grids, sparse or low-rank tensors, baked voxel caches, polygon rasterization, and improved transmittance estimators. These systems may retain NeRF-style color and density semantics, but the foundational method's defining implementation is the continuous MLP queried along rays and differentiated through volumetric compositing. A compact statement of the complete method is therefore: NeRF learns F_Θ:(x,d)↦(σ,c) as a per-scene continuous neural field, samples (x,d) on camera rays, converts density over each interval into alpha, composites view-dependent colors from front to back using accumulated transmittance, and backpropagates photometric error between rendered and observed pixels. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency coordinate features, while coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling concentrates the fine network's evaluations where the coarse renderer expects visible contributions. Together these components define the foundational NeRF representation and its differentiable volume-rendering formulation. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison in this review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than a leaderboard of later accelerators: (1) the learned representation and supervision condition, (2) the differentiable rendering computation used during training and inference, and (3) the two implementation refinements—positional encoding and hierarchical sampling—that the original paper identifies as necessary for high-resolution complex scenes. The available frozen sources support comparisons of mechanisms and reported qualitative outcomes, but they do not provide a matched table of original NeRF datasets, baselines, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS values, and training settings in the selected excerpts. Therefore, numerical rankings across foundational NeRF and later systems should not be inferred from these snippets alone. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd]

Under the representation dimension, the original NeRF experiment setup is per-scene optimization: a fully connected network is fitted to a sparse set of input views with known camera poses, and the same scene function is later queried to synthesize novel views. Its input is a continuous 5D coordinate—three spatial dimensions and two viewing-direction dimensions—and its outputs are density and view-dependent radiance. This is not directly comparable in learning regime to pixelNeRF, which conditions a NeRF on one or few input images through a fully convolutional architecture and learns a scene prior across multiple scenes; nor to HyperNeRF, whose experimental target is dynamic/non-rigid interpolation and fixed-moment novel-view synthesis rather than the original static-scene setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:5ccb35148c9e]

Under the rendering dimension, the common operation is ray casting followed by differentiable volumetric compositing. During training, rays from training poses are sampled, the network predicts σ_i and c_i at points along each ray, transmittance and alpha are computed from density and interval width, and the rendered color is compared with the observed image. A later exposition states the same discrete assumption: field values are treated as piecewise constant around each sample, and N samples approximate the continuous volume-rendering integral. This matched image-formation path means that pixel gradients can reach both color and density without explicit 3D labels; it also means that methods using rasterized polygons, explicit surfaces plus shaders, or reflection-ray transport are not like-for-like render-cost comparisons merely because they synthesize novel views. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:831b640ff374] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f]

The original paper's own ablation logic separates the basic continuous field and renderer from the refinements needed for state-of-the-art quality. It explicitly reports that the core components are not sufficient for its best high-resolution results and introduces positional encoding plus hierarchical volume sampling. Positional encoding changes the network input so high-frequency geometry and appearance are easier to represent; hierarchical sampling changes sample allocation by using normalized coarse weights as a piecewise-constant depth PDF and adding fine samples through inverse transform sampling. Thus, within the original method, the fair comparison is not “MLP field versus volume renderer,” but base components versus the same renderer augmented with high-frequency encoding and coarse-to-fine sample placement. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53]

The coarse and fine stages use the same rendering rule but different sample budgets and allocation. The coarse network is evaluated at N_c stratified samples; its weights are w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)). After normalization, those weights define where N_f additional samples are drawn. The fine network is evaluated at the union of first- and second-stage samples, and the final ray color uses all N_c+N_f samples. The paper notes that this is related to importance sampling in goal, but it is implemented as a nonuniform discretization of the integration domain rather than independent Monte Carlo estimates. Consequently, reported gains from hierarchical sampling should be understood as gains from concentrating network evaluations near expected visible content, not from replacing alpha compositing with another rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f]

The original NeRF evidence reported in the selected abstract is qualitative at the level available here: the authors state that the method achieves state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis for complex scenes and outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis work. The excerpt does not include the benchmark names, baseline identities, sample counts, per-scene training schedules, or numerical PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS measurements needed to reproduce that comparison. Those details are therefore not supplied in this chapter. What is directly supported is the experimental mechanism: posed images supervise a differentiably rendered continuous 5D field, and the paper claims photorealistic rendering of complicated geometry and appearance when positional encoding and hierarchical sampling are used. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02]

Comparisons with mip-NeRF must be scoped to anti-aliasing rather than treated as a test of the foundational volume-rendering identity. Original NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and point-like coordinates; mip-NeRF instead renders anti-aliased conical frustums and uses integrated positional encoding to encode continuously valued scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF reports a 17% reduction in average error; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced in that paper, it reports a 60% reduction. It also reports matching a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster, while being about 7% faster and half the parameter count of NeRF. These figures come from mip-NeRF's scale/aliasing setting and should not be read as generic superiority of frustum rendering for every NeRF task. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:134e66531564] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:8cf251239f23] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:712dfa864837]

Efficiency-oriented systems expose a different trade-off dimension: they often alter the representation or rendering pipeline to reduce the hundreds of MLP evaluations per pixel required by vanilla ray marching. SNeRG bakes NeRF into a sparse neural radiance grid and uses deferred lightweight-MLP shading; the MobileNeRF excerpt reports that this precomputation/deferred approach increases rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but also says SNeRG still ray marches sparse volumetric textures and needs substantial GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead uses textured polygons, z-buffer rasterization, and a fragment-shader MLP to exploit conventional graphics hardware. These results address interactive deployment and are not matched ablations of the original 5D MLP under identical storage and quality constraints. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:a6cd578a7035]

Other reported runtime numbers are likewise task- and system-specific. EvaSurf combines an efficient surface-based model, multi-view supervision, implicit view-dependent texture with Gaussian lobes, and a lightweight shader; it reports 1–2 hours of training on one GPU, mobile rendering above 40 FPS, and a 40–50 MB rendering package. DNMP parameterizes urban scenes with deformable neural mesh primitives and reports 2.07 ms per 1,000 pixels, 110 MB peak memory per 1,000 pixels, and a lightweight version at 0.61 versus Instant-NGP's 0.71 ms per 1,000 pixels. Because these methods use explicit surfaces or mesh primitives and different datasets/tasks, their FPS, memory, and millisecond figures are not directly interchangeable with original NeRF's per-ray MLP evaluation cost. [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:ed5c2ff4a7e2] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:951b470f41c2] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:ef5225226b22]

Across these comparisons, the experimentally defining features of foundational NeRF are the per-scene continuous 5D MLP, posed-image supervision, density-and-directional-color queries, and transmittance-weighted differentiable compositing. The strongest supported conclusion is mechanistic: positional encoding and hierarchical sampling were added by the original authors because the basic field and renderer did not attain their target quality, while later scale-aware, baked, voxel, polygon, mesh-primitive, and image-conditioned systems change one or more of the sampling primitive, storage structure, rendering hardware path, or learning regime. The selected evidence does not justify a universal numerical ranking; matched datasets, metrics, and resource budgets would be required for that. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The open-problems discussion here follows the review's existing organizing choice: limitations are grouped by whether they arise from the foundational NeRF representation, the differentiable volume-rendering computation, the static per-scene learning setup, or extensions needed for scale and deployment. These are source-supported trade-offs of the cited methods, not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering research. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8]

The first foundational limitation is computational. Rendering a pixel requires casting a ray and evaluating the neural network at many 3D sample positions to approximate the volume-rendering integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as requiring hundreds of network evaluations per pixel and identify repeated ray marching through a large MLP as the barrier to real-time or interactive rendering. This cost affects both optimization and novel-view generation: the same differentiable integration that enables supervision from posed images also makes training and inference sample intensive. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:4baacae88add] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:ed5c2ff4a7e2] Hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling mitigates but does not remove this cost. It allocates more samples to regions expected to contribute to the image by converting coarse compositing weights into a depth distribution and drawing additional fine samples from it. The method therefore improves sample placement relative to uniform or stratified evaluation, but the fine renderer still evaluates a network at the union of coarse and second-stage samples. It is an importance-like allocation strategy within volume rendering, not a constant-time representation or a replacement for ray integration. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_optimizing_a_neural_radiance_field:0:cbb6773b9f53:claim:22f5baed348f]

A second limitation is that the continuous MLP representation is not automatically efficient to deploy on conventional graphics hardware. Baked sparse voxel grids can accelerate rendering, but the SNeRG description notes that such grids still require ray marching and substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF instead moves to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization with a small fragment-shader MLP, while DNMP uses deformable mesh primitives to obtain rasterization efficiency. These systems illustrate a trade-off: preserving the original continuous volumetric field is convenient for differentiable view synthesis, whereas interactive hardware deployment often motivates changing the data structure and rendering path. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:2c111e872913] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0132fecc472f] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:ef5225226b22]

The base representation also does not provide an explicit, readily editable surface. NeRF stores density and view-dependent radiance as a continuous function queried along rays, rather than a triangle mesh or another explicit geometry object. Later work notes that NeRF-style fields can have high rendering quality but structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation. This does not mean surfaces cannot be extracted from some NeRF variants; rather, explicit editing, mesh export, and physical geometry tasks are not directly supplied by the foundational density-and-radiance MLP. [E:arxiv:2507.11971:abstract:claim:2730a1af752f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] View-dependent radiance creates a related geometry-appearance ambiguity. Although density is nominally a function of 3D position and color is a function of position and direction, the network can explain some image changes using view-dependent color rather than uniquely correct geometry. Work on the shape-radiance ambiguity analyzes this possibility, and VDN-NeRF states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting. Its response is to normalize or distill view-dependent information so geometry is less affected, without changing the volume-rendering pipeline; this confirms that simply adding c(x,d) does not disentangle shape, material, illumination, and motion. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:cc17a11de600] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:19e1b65754b8] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02]

The original emitted-radiance model also has limited physical scope. It can represent direction-dependent color such as simple specular appearance, but it does not explicitly trace reflection rays or decompose outgoing radiance into materials and lighting. Surface-based inverse-rendering systems can recover meshes, materials, and lighting, but the MobileNeRF excerpt notes a significant loss in view-synthesis quality for that class of approach and difficulty with expensive global illumination on mobile hardware. Conversely, later reflection-aware NeRF work adds traced reflection rays because expensive direct neural radiance queries and consistent nearby reflections remain difficult. These are extensions beyond the original c(x,d) parameterization. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:4:77bed4edf38c:claim:c24d236a6b0d] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:62a1e5ae8a8d]

Multiscale viewing is another unresolved property of the original point-ray formulation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and point-like 5D coordinates. Mip-NeRF reports that this can yield blur or aliasing when training and testing images observe content at different scales; simply casting more rays is expensive because every extra ray multiplies MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical frustums and integrated positional encoding reduce aliasing in that paper, while Mip-VoG later pursues explicit multiscale grids for real-time anti-aliasing. Thus, the foundational renderer integrates a ray but does not itself prefilter the spatial footprint of a pixel. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:134e66531564] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:8cf251239f23] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:644db93cbf81] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:5bad30e8f677]

The learning setting is restrictive as well. Foundational NeRF optimizes a separate network for each scene from posed images. PixelNeRF identifies two consequences of this regime: many calibrated views and significant optimization time are required for the original scene-specific approach. Its image-conditioned, cross-scene architecture is designed to predict a scene representation from one or few views, but that is a different feed-forward learning problem with its own generalization and uncertainty challenges. Therefore, sparse-view or single-image reconstruction should not be treated as solved by the original per-scene optimization. [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:3ce231ddce04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:8181648b99c2] The static-scene assumption is also part of the foundational boundary. The original 5D field contains position and viewing direction but no time or deformation coordinate. HyperNeRF motivates its higher-dimensional model by explaining that deformation-based dynamic NeRFs use continuous mappings into a canonical space and therefore struggle with topological changes, which require discontinuity. HyperNeRF's per-image slices through a higher-dimensional field target dynamic interpolation and fixed-moment novel-view synthesis, indicating that changing topology and non-rigid motion are outside the base static formulation. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:5ccb35148c9e] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:a3e67915cb53]

Finally, architectural acceleration introduces its own trade-offs rather than a single universal solution. PVD describes plain MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and their compositions as competing NeRF structures with distinct trade-offs; it specifically notes that hash-table representations train and render faster but lack clear geometric meaning for spatial-relation-aware editing. Hyb-NeRF similarly combines encodings to balance speed, quality, aliasing, and memory. The open problem is therefore not merely making NeRF faster: practitioners must jointly choose representation interpretability, storage, rendering hardware, multiscale behavior, editability, and view-synthesis fidelity. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:59ff77f29e8b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6b2c3eff679] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:c317f01e8195] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:section:abstract:1:80a6a4758916:claim:2e11b9886350]

## Conclusion

The core answer is therefore a continuous per-scene neural radiance field coupled to a transmittance-weighted ray integral. Density supplies opacity-like termination probability, while direction-conditioned radiance permits non-Lambertian appearance; the discrete renderer turns sampled density and color into a differentiable pixel prediction. The main trade-off is that this formulation enables photometric optimization and 3D-consistent view synthesis, but requires many network evaluations along rays, uses a static scene-specific model, and does not by itself provide explicit surfaces, material–lighting decomposition, or multiscale prefiltering. claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.

RayGauss provides a physically consistent formulation of emitted radiance c and density σ, decomposed with Gaussian functions associated with Spherical Gaussians/Harmonics for all-frequency colorimetric representation.
RayGauss introduces a differentiable ray casting method for irregularly distributed Gaussians that integrates radiance fields slab by slab and leverages a BVH structure.

fact_fields.method: slab-by-slab radiance field integration with BVH-accelerated ray casting

claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves superior rendering quality compared to the state-of-the-art while maintaining reasonable training times.
RayGauss represents radiance fields as a weighted sum of locally supported elliptical basis functions with optimizable positions, orientations, and scales.
RayGauss combines spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG) with elliptical basis functions to represent high-frequency color variations such as specular reflections.
RayGauss's volume ray casting algorithm accumulates colorimetric properties along the ray in slabs of space corresponding to multiple samples, rather than processing individual samples.
RayGauss's ray casting algorithm and its backpropagation are implemented on GPU using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) with the OptiX library.

The classic volumetric rendering equation used by NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting defines ray color C(r) as the integral along the ray of emitted radiance c(r(t), d) weighted by density σ(r(t)) and transmittance T(t).

NeRF's differentiable volume ray casting algorithm computes a discretized version of the volumetric rendering equation using N samples along the ray, assuming fields are piecewise constant in each sample neighborhood.
3D Gaussian Splatting's splatting algorithm causes artifacts such as flickering when deviating from training views, due to sudden changes in primitive ordering.

claim_records.text: NeRFMeshing distills a trained NeRF volumetric 3D representation into a Signed Surface Approximation Network (SSAN) to enable easy extraction of 3D mesh and appearance.
NeRFMeshing's final 3D mesh is physically accurate and can be rendered in real time on an array of devices.
NeRFMeshing produces meshes with neural colors having accurate geometry that can be rendered in real time on commodity hardware.
SSAN estimates a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) and a feature appearance field, using the NeRF approximated geometry and training views for distillation.
NeRFMeshing does not rely on a fixed grid template during training, enabling reconstruction at any arbitrary resolution afterwards.
NeRFMeshing relies only on NeRF networks trained from images, without requiring additional input modalities such as depth.
NeRFMeshing can be leveraged together with any NeRF, without requiring modifications to the NeRF architecture.
NeRFMeshing's extracted 3D meshes can be integrated in graphics and simulation pipelines, and preserve view-dependent effects and reflections from neural radiance fields.

NeRFMeshing extracts meshes from scenes including Chair, Hot-dog, Lego from the Blender dataset and Garden from the MipNeRF 360 dataset, and supports physics-based simulations such as cloth falling on objects from the Blender Synthetic dataset.

NeRF methods often approximate object surfaces by dense regions of the volume instead of surfaces of zero thickness, because NeRFs are optimized for view synthesis rather than accurate underlying geometry.

claim_records.text: The NeRF method optimizes a continuous volumetric scene function using a sparse set of input views to synthesize novel views of complex scenes.

The NeRF scene representation uses a fully-connected non-convolutional deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input, and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF synthesizes views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.
The NeRF method demonstrates results that outperform prior work on neural rendering and view synthesis.
The volume density σ(x) in NeRF can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.

The expected color C(r) of camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed as the integral over the ray of accumulated transmittance T(t) multiplied by volume density σ(r(t)) and emitted color c(r(t), d), where T(t) = exp(−∫tn^t σ(r(s))ds).
Rendering a view from the continuous NeRF requires estimating the color integral C(r) for a camera ray traced through each pixel of the desired virtual camera.
The NeRF MLP FΘ maps input (x, d) to output (c, σ), where x is 3D location, d is 3D Cartesian unit viewing direction vector, c is emitted RGB color, and σ is volume density.
To encourage multiview consistency, the NeRF MLP predicts volume density σ as a function of only location x, while predicting RGB color c as a function of both location and viewing direction.
The NeRF MLP first processes input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer, outputting σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the density-processing layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer using ReLU activation and 128 channels that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

NeRF uses two simultaneously optimized networks, a coarse network and a fine network, to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.

fact_fields.method: hierarchical volume sampling with coarse and fine networks

claim_records.text: The coarse network is first evaluated at Nc locations sampled using stratified sampling along each camera ray.

The coarse network's alpha composited color is rewritten as a weighted sum of sampled colors along the ray, with weights wi = Ti(1 − exp(−σiδi)), and normalized weights ŵi = wi / Σwj produce a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray.

A second set of Nf locations is sampled from the piecewise-constant PDF using inverse transform sampling, and the fine network is evaluated at the union of the first and second sets of samples to compute the final rendered color using all Nc+Nf samples.

fact_fields.method: inverse transform sampling for fine network

claim_records.text: Two improvements are introduced to NeRF to enable representing high-resolution complex scenes: positional encoding of input coordinates to assist the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure to efficiently sample this high-frequency representation.
Directly operating the NeRF MLP on raw xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.

Reformulating the NeRF MLP as a composition FΘ = F'Θ ◦ γ, where γ is a fixed mapping from R into a higher dimensional space R^{2L}, significantly improves performance compared to directly operating on input coordinates.

fact_fields.method: positional encoding reformulation FΘ = F'Θ ◦ γ

claim_records.text: The positional encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L-1} πp), cos(2^{L-1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [-1,1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [-1,1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for positional encoding of spatial coordinates γ(x), and L = 4 is used for positional encoding of viewing directions γ(d).

claim_records.text: Traditional NeRFs rely on specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF introduces a NeRF representation based on textured polygons that can synthesize novel images efficiently with standard rendering pipelines.
In MobileNeRF, the NeRF is represented as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

MobileNeRF renders polygons with a z-buffer to produce an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color.

fact_fields.method: z-buffer polygon rasterization + fragment shader MLP

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF achieves interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms including mobile phones by utilizing the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline which provides massive pixel-level parallelism.

Traditional NeRF implementations evaluate a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance, making the rendering process far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude compared to traditional NeRF.

fact_fields.method: SNeRG sparse voxel grid precomputation and deferred rendering

claim_records.text: SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce features for each pixel, so it cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity GPUs.
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.
MobileNeRF consumes less memory than SNeRG by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling it to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all tested devices, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes because they are represented as simple triangle meshes.

Light field and Lumigraph representations store a dense grid of images enabling real-time rendering of high quality scenes, but support only limited camera freedom and incur significant storage overhead.

Point-based neural rendering representations increase quality by jointly refining scene geometry while training post-processing networks, but require powerful desktop GPUs and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Differentiable inverse-rendering methods such as DefTet and NVDiffRec can extract explicit triangle meshes but incur a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting for differentiable inverse-rendering methods, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF caches outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and results in higher view-synthesis quality than differentiable inverse-rendering methods.
Rendering a traditional NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model can be distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model at a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations, from shallower to deeper, to enable fast architecture conversions.
PVD employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem during distillation.
PVD is empirically validated on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.

In the Family and Barn scenes from the TanksAndTemples dataset, a NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours.
PVD uses loss on intermediate volume representations including output of φ1*, color and density alongside the final rendered RGB volume to accelerate distillation.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate training based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.
PVD employs special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that is capable of creating color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF leverages an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF is currently restricted to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.

claim_records.text: The unconditional diffusion model for volumetric field reconstruction is trained on a novel benchmark dataset comprising 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: Unconditional diffusion model trained on latent codes of a diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation

claim_records.text: A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space for the reconstruction pipeline.
The diffusion model is trained on latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation for volumetric field decoding.

Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, requiring dozens to hundreds of views to adequately constrain object parameters.

fact_fields.method: Differentiable rendering for volumetric material parameter recovery

claim_records.text: The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field, including controlled variations in the diffusion step by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation.

fact_fields.method: Diffusion prior-guided Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR)

claim_records.text: The 3D density field can be trained solely on the diffusion prior, not requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects, as the renderer uses the prior for density distribution but not for appearance.
The key contributions include a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.

The Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer, which is claimed to be the first such integration.
The proposed approach is demonstrated across various tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

fact_fields.method: Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) with diffusion prior and PDVR

claims: The unconditional diffusion model for volumetric field reconstruction is trained on a novel benchmark dataset comprising 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.
A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space for the reconstruction pipeline.
The diffusion model is trained on latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation for volumetric field decoding.

Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, requiring dozens to hundreds of views to adequately constrain object parameters.

The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field, including controlled variations in the diffusion step by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation.

The 3D density field can be trained solely on the diffusion prior, not requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects, as the renderer uses the prior for density distribution but not for appearance.
The key contributions include a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.

The Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer, which is claimed to be the first such integration.
The proposed approach is demonstrated across various tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

claim_records.text: NeRF's rendering procedure samples a scene with a single ray per pixel and may produce renderings that are excessively blurred or aliased when training or testing images observe scene content at different resolutions.
The straightforward supersampling solution of rendering with multiple rays per pixel is impractical for NeRF because rendering each ray requires querying a multilayer perceptron hundreds of times.

fact_fields.method: supersampling by rendering multiple rays per pixel

claim_records.text: Mip-NeRF extends NeRF to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale by efficiently rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays.
Mip-NeRF is 7% faster than NeRF and half the size.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% on the dataset presented with NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 60% on a challenging multiscale variant of the NeRF dataset.
Mip-NeRF matches the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22x faster.
Mip-NeRF merges the separate coarse and fine MLPs used by NeRF for hierarchical sampling into a single MLP, resulting in approximately 7% speed improvement and half as many parameters as NeRF.
NeRF trained on full-resolution images produces photorealistic renderings at new view locations only at the resolution or scale of the training images.
Training a NeRF on multi-resolution images ameliorates aliasing slightly but results in poor quality renderings across scales: blur at full resolution and jaggies at low resolutions.
Mip-NeRF trained on multi-resolution images produces photorealistic renderings across different scales.

claim_records.text: Fourier PlenOctrees suffer from artifacts introduced by the involved compression when combined with recent state-of-the-art techniques for training static per-frame NeRF models.

The proposed novel density encoding adapts Fourier-based compression to the characteristics of the transfer function used by the underlying volume rendering procedure, leading to a substantial reduction of artifacts in the dynamic model.

fact_fields.method: novel density encoding for Fourier PlenOctrees

claim_records.text: The proposed training data augmentation relaxes the periodicity assumption of the Fourier compression.
During FPO construction, compression is performed on encoded densities σ' = e_comp(e_log(σ)), where the encoding consists of a component-dependent part and a logarithmic part.

The proposed component-dependent and logarithmic density encoding allows better reconstruction of original densities without fine-tuning than can be achieved with only DFT and IDFT as proposed for FPOs.

fact_fields.method: component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT only

claim_records.text: Non-negative density values σ are logarithmically encoded as e_log(σ) = log(σ + 1) before applying the DFT.
The logarithmic density encoding focuses approximation on densities near or equal to zero by mapping larger values closer together while keeping smaller values almost unchanged.
The encoded density sequences are easier to approximate with a low-frequency Fourier basis exploiting the properties of the transfer function.

The logarithmic density encoding allows the L2-error in fine-tuning to be larger for encoded high values than without logarithmic encoding, focusing optimization on more important parts of the reconstruction.

Fourier PlenOctrees extend ordinary PlenOctrees, which are limited to static scenes, by combining them with the Fourier transform to enable handling time-variant density and SH-based radiance efficiently.
PlenOctrees use a hierarchical octree structure of density and view-dependent radiance in terms of spherical harmonics to entirely avoid network evaluations.

claim_records.text: Existing NeRF-based single-image novel view synthesis approaches condition NeRF on local image features, projecting points to the input image plane and aggregating 2D features to perform volume rendering.
Under severe occlusion, the projection-based NeRF approach fails to resolve uncertainty, resulting in blurry renderings that lack details.

fact_fields.method: projection-based NeRF single-image novel view synthesis

claim_records.text: NerfDiff addresses the occlusion-related blurriness issue by distilling knowledge of a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF through synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff's NeRF-guided distillation algorithm simultaneously generates 3D consistent virtual views from the CDM samples and finetunes the NeRF based on the improved virtual views.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on challenging datasets including ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D.

Differentiable rendering methods like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) use differentiable volume rendering or surface-based representation to generate high-fidelity scenes.
Existing NeRF and differentiable rendering methods require excessive runtime for rendering, making them impractical for daily applications.

EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf employs a lightweight neural shader alongside explicit geometry and implicit texture to reduce computation expense and support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.
EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf can be trained in just 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS (Frames Per Second).
The final package required for EvaSurf rendering takes up only 40-50 MB.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve impressive view synthesis results for a variety of capture settings, including 360 capture of bounded scenes and forward-facing capture of bounded and unbounded scenes.

NeRF fits multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) representing view-invariant opacity and view-dependent color volumes to a set of training images, and samples novel views based on volume rendering techniques.
Radiance fields have potential ambiguities, namely the shape-radiance ambiguity, and NeRF's success in avoiding such ambiguities is analyzed in this technical report.
A parametrization issue is involved in applying NeRF to 360 captures of objects within large-scale, unbounded 3D scenes.
The proposed method improves view synthesis fidelity in the challenging scenario of 360 captures of objects within large-scale, unbounded 3D scenes.
Code for the method is available at https://github.com/Kai-46/nerfplusplus.
