claim_records.text: The rendering scheme in neural radiance field (NeRF) is effective in rendering a pixel by casting a ray into the scene.
NeRF yields blurred rendering results when the training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if the test images are taken in distant views.
Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information.
Mip-NeRF is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG includes a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.

claim_records.text: pixelNeRF is a learning framework that predicts a continuous neural scene representation conditioned on one or few input images.
pixelNeRF introduces an architecture that conditions a NeRF on image inputs in a fully convolutional manner.

The fully convolutional conditioning design of pixelNeRF allows the network to be trained across multiple scenes to learn a scene prior, enabling feed-forward novel view synthesis from a sparse set of views as few as one.
Leveraging the volume rendering approach of NeRF, pixelNeRF can be trained directly from images with no explicit 3D supervision.
pixelNeRF is evaluated on ShapeNet benchmarks for single image novel view synthesis tasks with held-out objects as well as entire unseen categories.
pixelNeRF is demonstrated on multi-object ShapeNet scenes and real scenes from the DTU dataset.
In all evaluated cases, pixelNeRF outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines for novel view synthesis and single image 3D reconstruction.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of CLIP.
CLIP-NeRF provides a unified framework that allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved by applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing.
The code mappers of CLIP-NeRF are trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to the latent codes for manipulation to enable editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF is evaluated by extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images, and provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing.

claim_records.text: UE4-NeRF partitions each large scene into different sub-NeRFs to support real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.
UE4-NeRF initializes polygonal meshes by constructing multiple regular octahedra within the scene, with vertices of the polygonal faces continuously optimized during training.
Drawing inspiration from Level of Detail (LOD) techniques, UE4-NeRF trains meshes of varying levels of detail for different observation levels.
When combined with the rasterization pipeline in Unreal Engine 4 (UE4), UE4-NeRF achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes at 4K resolution with a frame rate of up to 43 FPS.

claim_records.text: Rendering within UE4 facilitates scene editing in subsequent stages for the UE4-NeRF system.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes, where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF considers time as an additional input to the system, and splits the learning process into two main stages: one that encodes the scene into a canonical space and another that maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
Once the networks are trained, D-NeRF can render novel images, controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus, the object movement.
The effectiveness of D-NeRF is demonstrated on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.

claim_records.text: NeRF can produce photorealistic renderings of unseen viewpoints when many input views are available, but its performance drops significantly when this number is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input scenarios are caused by errors in the estimated scene geometry, and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
The proposed method regularizes the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and anneals the ray sampling space during training.
The proposed method additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
The proposed model outperforms not only other methods that optimize over a single scene, but in many cases also conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF models scenes with an MLP and volume rendering for novel view synthesis, but overfits when given fewer known views in few-shot view synthesis.
Trivially reducing the number of model parameters alleviates the overfitting issue in few-shot view synthesis, but at the cost of missing details.
The proposed multi-input MLP (mi-MLP) incorporates the inputs (location and viewing direction) of the vanilla MLP into each layer to prevent overfitting without harming detailed synthesis.
The proposed framework models colors and volume density separately and presents two regularization terms to further reduce artifacts.

fact_fields.method: mi-MLP framework with separate color/volume density modeling and two regularization terms

claim_records.text: The proposed mi-MLP boosts the PSNR of the baseline from 14.73 to 24.23 on multiple datasets.
The overall framework achieves state-of-the-art results on a wide range of benchmarks.

claim_records.text: Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific and lack universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
All surveyed 3D representations inherently struggle with the trade-off between data complexity and fidelity.

The novel 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized tree-structured proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent NeRF works that improve rendering of detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Recent NeRF specular appearance techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The proposed NeRF-Casting model casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors, which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.
The proposed NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: The presented Nerfies method is the first method capable of photorealistically reconstructing deformable scenes using photos/videos captured casually from mobile phones.
The Nerfies approach augments neural radiance fields by optimizing an additional continuous volumetric deformation field that warps each observed point into a canonical 5D NeRF.
NeRF-like deformation fields are prone to local minima during optimization.
The proposed coarse-to-fine optimization method for coordinate-based models enables more robust optimization for NeRF-like deformation fields.

fact_fields.method: coarse-to-fine optimization method for coordinate-based models

claim_records.text: The proposed elastic regularization of the deformation field, adapted from principles in geometry processing and physical simulation, further improves optimization robustness for NeRF-like models.
The Nerfies method can turn casually captured selfie photos/videos into deformable NeRF models that allow for photorealistic renderings of the subject from arbitrary viewpoints.
Evaluation of the Nerfies method used time-synchronized data collected via a rig with two mobile phones, yielding train/validation images of the same pose at different viewpoints.
The Nerfies method faithfully reconstructs non-rigidly deforming scenes and reproduces unseen views with high fidelity.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.
SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding.
Global features in SHERF enhance the information extracted from the single input image and complement the information missing from the partial 2D observation.
Point-level features in SHERF provide strong clues of 3D human structure.
Pixel-aligned features in SHERF preserve more fine-grained details.
SHERF designs a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: NeRF uses straight rays and fails to deal with complicated light path changes caused by refraction and reflection.
NeRF's limitation of failing to handle refraction and reflection prevents it from successfully synthesizing transparent or specular objects.
The NeRRF method takes the object silhouette as input to reconstruct the geometry of non-Lambertian objects.
NeRRF utilizes marching tetrahedra with a progressive encoding to reconstruct the geometry of non-Lambertian objects.
NeRRF models refraction and reflection effects of the object in a unified framework using Fresnel terms.
NeRRF proposes a virtual cone supersampling technique to achieve efficient and effective anti-aliasing.
NeRRF is benchmarked on different shapes, backgrounds and Fresnel terms on both real-world and synthetic datasets.
NeRRF's rendering results are qualitatively and quantitatively benchmarked for editing applications including material editing, object replacement/insertion, and environment illumination estimation.

claim_records.text: Most current NeRF methods require intensive resources due to ray marching-based rendering.

DNMP is a flexible and compact neural variant of classic mesh representation that enjoys both the efficiency of rasterization-based rendering and the powerful neural representation capability for photo-realistic image synthesis.
A DNMP consists of a set of connected deformable mesh vertices with paired vertex features to parameterize the geometry and radiance information of a local area.
DNMP enforces the shape of each primitive to be decoded from a relatively low-dimensional latent space to constrain optimization degrees of freedom and lower storage budgets.
DNMP decodes rendering colors from vertex features (interpolated with rasterization) by a view-dependent MLP.
The DNMP method achieves leading performance for novel view synthesis in urban scenarios.
The DNMP representation enables fast rendering at 2.07ms per 1k pixels.
The DNMP representation has low peak memory usage of 110MB per 1k pixels.
The lightweight version of DNMP can run 33 times faster than vanilla NeRFs.
The lightweight version of DNMP has a rendering speed of 0.61ms per 1k pixels, comparable to Instant-NGP's 0.71ms per 1k pixels.

claim_records.text: Existing NeRF-like models struggle on unbounded scenes, often producing blurry or low-resolution renderings, slow training, and artifacts due to inherent ambiguity of reconstructing a large scene from a small set of images.
mip-NeRF 360 is an extension of mip-NeRF that uses a non-linear scene parameterization, online distillation, and a novel distortion-based regularizer to address unbounded scene challenges.
mip-NeRF 360 reduces mean-squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF.
mip-NeRF 360 produces realistic synthesized views and detailed depth maps for highly intricate, unbounded real-world scenes.

claim_records.text: The presented method synthesizes novel views of complex scenes by interpolating a sparse set of nearby views.

The core network architecture includes a multilayer perceptron and a ray transformer that estimates radiance and volume density at continuous 5D locations (3D spatial locations and 2D viewing directions), drawing appearance information on the fly from multiple source views.
The method learns a generic view interpolation function that generalizes to novel scenes, unlike neural scene representation work that optimizes per-scene functions for rendering.
Images are rendered using classic volume rendering, which is fully differentiable and allows training using only multi-view posed images as supervision.
Experiments show the method outperforms recent novel view synthesis methods that also seek to generalize to novel scenes.
If fine-tuned on each scene, the method is competitive with state-of-the-art single-scene neural rendering methods.

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF is a method to train neural radiance fields for better geometry under non-Lambertian surface and dynamic lighting conditions that cause significant variation in the radiance of a point when viewed from different angles.

VDN-NeRF normalizes view-dependence by distilling invariant information already encoded in the learned NeRFs, rather than explicitly modeling the underlying factors that result in the view-dependent phenomenon.

fact_fields.method: view-dependence normalization via distilling invariant information encoded in learned NeRFs

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF jointly trains NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization to attain quality geometry.

fact_fields.method: joint training of NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization

claim_records.text: Experiments show that even though shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable, the proposed normalization can minimize its effect on geometry, which essentially aligns the optimal capacity needed for explaining view-dependent variations.
VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

joint training of NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization

Experiments show that even though shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable, the proposed normalization can minimize its effect on geometry, which essentially aligns the optimal capacity needed for explaining view-dependent variations.
VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

claim_records.text: NeuDA is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity implicit surface reconstruction.
NeuDA maintains hierarchical anchor grids where each vertex stores a 3D position (anchor) instead of a direct embedding (feature).
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.
Experiments on the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.

Previous differentiable ray casting-based implicit surface reconstruction works IDR and NeuS overlook spatial context in 3D space when predicting and rendering surfaces, and may fail to capture sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures.

claim_records.text: HollowNeRF delivers comparable rendering quality to Instant-NGP while utilizing just 31% of the parameters.
HollowNeRF can achieve a PSNR accuracy gain of up to 1dB using only 56% of the parameters.

HollowNeRF trains a coarse 3D saliency mask that guides efficient feature pruning, and employs an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) pruner to sparsify the 3D saliency mask during training.
By exploiting the sparsity in the 3D scene to redistribute hash collisions, HollowNeRF improves rendering quality while using a fraction of the parameters of comparable state-of-the-art solutions.

The method demonstrates state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering on several established datasets.

assertions.source_quote: Foundational NeRF addresses static novel-view synthesis by optimizing, for each scene, a fully connected MLP that maps a continuous 5D coordinate—3D position plus viewing direction—to position-dependent volume density and view-dependent RGB radiance. Camera rays are sampled in 3D, and pixel color is formed by differentiable alpha compositing: each interval contributes its color weighted by alpha and accumulated transmittance. This makes density and color trainable from posed images without explicit 3D supervision. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are the original refinements that support high-frequency detail and allocate samples toward visible content. assertions.source_quote: Images are formed by classical volume rendering made differentiable. For a camera ray r(t)=o+td bounded by near and far distances, NeRF integrates the radiance c(r(t),d) weighted by density σ(r(t)) and accumulated transmittance T(t), where T(t)=exp(−∫σ(r(s))ds). Density acts as the differential probability that the ray terminates at a point, and transmittance is the probability that the ray reaches that point without earlier termination. Because the rendered color is a differentiable composite of network outputs, NeRF can be optimized from posed 2D images alone without explicit 3D supervision. assertions.source_quote: For this review, the organizing choice is to separate three questions that foundational NeRF combines: what is represented, how a representation is rendered into an image, and what the optimization target is. The representation criterion asks whether a method stores geometry and appearance in a continuous coordinate-based field, an explicit grid, polygons, mesh primitives, or another data structure. The rendering criterion asks whether pixel color is produced by differentiable volume integration, rasterization, ray tracing, or a hybrid shader. The supervision criterion asks whether training is per-scene optimization from posed images or feed-forward prediction conditioned on images. These are comparison dimensions, not a claim that later work falls into a fixed number of categories. assertions.source_quote: Foundational NeRF belongs at the intersection of continuous neural fields and differentiable volume rendering: its MLP is a per-scene 5D function from position and viewing direction to density and radiance, and its image formation model integrates samples along each ray. This differs from methods whose primary representation is an explicit textured polygon mesh or deformable mesh primitive. MobileNeRF, for example, uses polygons carrying binary-opacity textures and feature vectors, then relies on z-buffered rasterization and a small view-dependent fragment shader; DNMP parameterizes local geometry and radiance with connected deformable mesh vertices and vertex features. Those approaches may preserve NeRF-style view synthesis, but they do not use the original continuous MLP-plus-ray-integral representation as their core storage. assertions.source_quote: Task scope is another boundary. The original NeRF objective is static-scene novel-view synthesis: optimize one scene representation from images and known poses, then render new camera views. PixelNeRF remains compatible with NeRF's volume-rendering supervision but changes the learning setting by conditioning a network on one or few input images and learning a cross-scene prior. HyperNeRF instead targets dynamic or non-rigid scenes and models per-image radiance fields as slices through a higher-dimensional field, addressing a limitation of continuous deformation fields when topology changes. These are extensions in input conditioning or time/configuration modeling, not alternative statements of the original static 5D field. assertions.source_quote: Finally, differentiable volume rendering should not be equated with every differentiable-rendering objective. Surface-based inverse rendering can optimize meshes, occupancy, materials, and lighting through differentiable rasterization or marching-tetrahedra pipelines; some later mobile reconstruction systems combine explicit surfaces, implicit textures, and lightweight shaders. Those methods may be trained from images and produce view-dependent appearance, but their image-formation path and geometric assumptions differ from NeRF's transmittance-weighted volumetric integral. The foundational NeRF classification is therefore narrow but precise: a continuous, per-scene, position-and-direction-conditioned radiance field, rendered by differentiable density-weighted compositing along camera rays. assertions.source_quote: The foundational NeRF mechanism is a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron optimized separately for one scene. Its learned function takes a 5D input consisting of spatial position x=(x,y,z) and viewing direction d, represented in the original paper through direction coordinates (θ,φ), and returns two kinds of quantities at that ray sample: a scalar volume density σ(x) and an emitted color c(x,d), typically RGB. The architectural split matters: density depends on position, whereas color depends on both position and viewing direction, allowing the same occupied location to have direction-dependent appearance. The original network is fully connected and non-convolutional; it is not a discrete mesh, voxel occupancy array, or image-to-3D predictor. assertions.source_quote: The physical interpretation of the field is volumetric rather than strictly surface based. At position x, σ(x) is interpreted as the differential probability that a ray terminates on an infinitesimal particle there. High density therefore behaves like opaque or strongly participating matter, while low or zero density permits the ray to continue. Unlike a hard binary surface, this formulation can represent soft occupancy and semi-transparent content through continuous density. Color is emitted radiance conditioned on view direction, which is how the model captures view-varying effects such as specular appearance without explicitly decomposing the scene into material and lighting parameters. assertions.source_quote: For rendering, a camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o, unit direction d, and near and far bounds t_n and t_f. NeRF defines the expected color of that ray as C(r)=∫_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d) dt. The term T(t)=exp(−∫_{t_n}^{t}σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: it gives the probability that the ray travels from the near bound to t without interacting earlier. The integrand therefore combines the probability of reaching a sample, the local probability of interacting there, and the radiance emitted back along the ray. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:4_volume_rendering_with_radiance_fields:0:5a5296e2578c:claim:287137519c02] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:b438346465f8]

assertions.source_quote: The continuous integral is not evaluated analytically. NeRF estimates it numerically by querying the MLP at discrete samples along each ray. A common discrete rendering form uses sample colors c_i, densities σ_i, and interval widths δ_i. The alpha value for interval i is α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i), and transmittance is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j)=Π_{j<i}(1−α_j). The rendered ray color is then Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i. This is alpha compositing over depth-ordered volumetric samples; because every operation—sampling coordinates, MLP evaluation, exponentials, products, and weighted summation—is differentiable, image reconstruction loss can update the field weights. assertions.source_quote: The original implementation uses stratified sampling for its initial set of ray samples. The near-to-far interval is divided into evenly spaced bins, and one sample is drawn uniformly from each bin. This deterministic stratification with within-bin randomness provides coverage across the ray while encouraging the network to learn a continuous representation rather than overfitting samples at exactly the same depths. These coarse samples are sufficient to define the basic renderer, but the original paper reports that the basic components alone do not reach its state-of-the-art quality; two refinements are introduced for high-resolution complex scenes. assertions.source_quote: The first refinement is positional encoding. Raw low-dimensional coordinates are passed through high-frequency sinusoidal mappings before entering the MLP. NeRF introduces this mapping because deep networks on low-dimensional coordinates can be biased toward smoother functions; the lifted coordinates make high-frequency variation in geometry and appearance easier to optimize. In the original architecture, positional encoding is applied to both spatial coordinates and viewing-direction coordinates, although the encoding bandwidth and network use differ according to the roles of position and direction. This is a representation/input transformation, not a change to the volume-rendering equation. In the original architecture, positional encoding is applied to both spatial coordinates and viewing-direction coordinates, although the encoding bandwidth and network use differ according to the roles of position and direction. This is a representation/input transformation, not a change to the volume-rendering equation. assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical sampling changes where computation is spent, not the underlying compositing rule. Free space and occluded regions generally receive low coarse weights, whereas visible density receives higher weights, so the second stage places more fine samples near content expected to affect the image. The paper explicitly distinguishes this from treating each sample as an independent Monte Carlo estimate of the whole integral: the normalized coarse weights define a nonuniform discretization of the ray interval. The coarse rendering is still supervised, so the first network learns weights useful for allocating the second network's samples. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:346233f4d2bd]

assertions.source_quote: Training follows the renderer. For a selected pixel, a ray is cast through the scene, field samples are rendered into a predicted RGB color, and that prediction is compared with the observed pixel color. In the coarse-to-fine system, the loss includes both the coarse and fine renderings; the original paper's objective is the sum of the coarse and fine mean-squared color errors over rays. Gradients propagate from the pixel loss through the discrete transmittance-weighted composition to the colors and densities predicted by the MLPs. Repeating this optimization over many posed views fits a single scene's continuous radiance field. assertions.source_quote: The original formulation also does not solve aliasing by construction. assertions.source_quote: A compact statement of the complete method is therefore: NeRF learns F_Θ:(x,d)↦(σ,c) as a per-scene continuous neural field, samples (x,d) on camera rays, converts density over each interval into alpha, composites view-dependent colors from front to back using accumulated transmittance, and backpropagates photometric error between rendered and observed pixels. Together these components define the foundational NeRF representation and its differentiable volume-rendering formulation. assertions.source_quote: Under the representation dimension, the original NeRF experiment setup is per-scene optimization: a fully connected network is fitted to a sparse set of input views with known camera poses, and the same scene function is later queried to synthesize novel views. Its input is a continuous 5D coordinate—three spatial dimensions and two viewing-direction dimensions—and its outputs are density and view-dependent radiance. This is not directly comparable in learning regime to pixelNeRF, which conditions a NeRF on one or few input images through a fully convolutional architecture and learns a scene prior across multiple scenes; nor to HyperNeRF, whose experimental target is dynamic/non-rigid interpolation and fixed-moment novel-view synthesis rather than the original static-scene setup. assertions.source_quote: Under the rendering dimension, the common operation is ray casting followed by differentiable volumetric compositing. assertions.source_quote: The original paper's own ablation logic separates the basic continuous field and renderer from the refinements needed for state-of-the-art quality. It explicitly reports that the core components are not sufficient for its best high-resolution results and introduces positional encoding plus hierarchical volume sampling. Positional encoding changes the network input so high-frequency geometry and appearance are easier to represent; hierarchical sampling changes sample allocation by using normalized coarse weights as a piecewise-constant depth PDF and adding fine samples through inverse transform sampling. Thus, within the original method, the fair comparison is not “MLP field versus volume renderer,” but base components versus the same renderer augmented with high-frequency encoding and coarse-to-fine sample placement. assertions.source_quote: Comparisons with mip-NeRF must be scoped to anti-aliasing rather than treated as a test of the foundational volume-rendering identity. Original NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and point-like coordinates; mip-NeRF instead renders anti-aliased conical frustums and uses integrated positional encoding to encode continuously valued scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF reports a 17% reduction in average error; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced in that paper, it reports a 60% reduction. It also reports matching a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster, while being about 7% faster and half the parameter count of NeRF. These figures come from mip-NeRF's scale/aliasing setting and should not be read as generic superiority of frustum rendering for every NeRF task. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency-oriented systems expose a different trade-off dimension: they often alter the representation or rendering pipeline to reduce the hundreds of MLP evaluations per pixel required by vanilla ray marching. SNeRG bakes NeRF into a sparse neural radiance grid and uses deferred lightweight-MLP shading; the MobileNeRF excerpt reports that this precomputation/deferred approach increases rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but also says SNeRG still ray marches sparse volumetric textures and needs substantial GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead uses textured polygons, z-buffer rasterization, and a fragment-shader MLP to exploit conventional graphics hardware. These results address interactive deployment and are not matched ablations of the original 5D MLP under identical storage and quality constraints. assertions.source_quote: The first foundational limitation is computational. Rendering a pixel requires casting a ray and evaluating the neural network at many 3D sample positions to approximate the volume-rendering integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as requiring hundreds of network evaluations per pixel and identify repeated ray marching through a large MLP as the barrier to real-time or interactive rendering. This cost affects both optimization and novel-view generation: the same differentiable integration that enables supervision from posed images also makes training and inference sample intensive. assertions.source_quote: The first foundational limitation is computational. Rendering a pixel requires casting a ray and evaluating the neural network at many 3D sample positions to approximate the volume-rendering integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as requiring hundreds of network evaluations per pixel and identify repeated ray marching through a large MLP as the barrier to real-time or interactive rendering. This cost affects both optimization and novel-view generation: the same differentiable integration that enables supervision from posed images also makes training and inference sample intensive. assertions.claim_text: The same differentiable integration makes training and inference sample intensive.
assertions.explanation: The context states that NeRF requires evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along each ray, which makes both training and inference sample intensive, as the same differentiable integration that enables supervision requires many samples per ray.

assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling mitigates but does not remove this cost. It allocates more samples to regions expected to contribute to the image by converting coarse compositing weights into a depth distribution and drawing additional fine samples from it. The method therefore improves sample placement relative to uniform or stratified evaluation, but the fine renderer still evaluates a network at the union of coarse and second-stage samples. It is an importance-like allocation strategy within volume rendering, not a constant-time representation or a replacement for ray integration. assertions.source_quote: A second limitation is that the continuous MLP representation is not automatically efficient to deploy on conventional graphics hardware. Baked sparse voxel grids can accelerate rendering, but the SNeRG description notes that such grids still require ray marching and substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF instead moves to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization with a small fragment-shader MLP, while DNMP uses deformable mesh primitives to obtain rasterization efficiency. These systems illustrate a trade-off: preserving the original continuous volumetric field is convenient for differentiable view synthesis, whereas interactive hardware deployment often motivates changing the data structure and rendering path. assertions.source_quote: The base representation also does not provide an explicit, readily editable surface. NeRF stores density and view-dependent radiance as a continuous function queried along rays, rather than a triangle mesh or another explicit geometry object. Later work notes that NeRF-style fields can have high rendering quality but structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation. This does not mean surfaces cannot be extracted from some NeRF variants; rather, explicit editing, mesh export, and physical geometry tasks are not directly supplied by the foundational density-and-radiance MLP. assertions.source_quote: View-dependent radiance creates a related geometry-appearance ambiguity. Although density is nominally a function of 3D position and color is a function of position and direction, the network can explain some image changes using view-dependent color rather than uniquely correct geometry. Work on the shape-radiance ambiguity analyzes this possibility, and VDN-NeRF states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting. Its response is to normalize or distill view-dependent information so geometry is less affected, without changing the volume-rendering pipeline; this confirms that simply adding c(x,d) does not disentangle shape, material, illumination, and motion. assertions.source_quote: The original emitted-radiance model also has limited physical scope. It can represent direction-dependent color such as simple specular appearance, but it does not explicitly trace reflection rays or decompose outgoing radiance into materials and lighting. Surface-based inverse-rendering systems can recover meshes, materials, and lighting, but the MobileNeRF excerpt notes a significant loss in view-synthesis quality for that class of approach and difficulty with expensive global illumination on mobile hardware. Conversely, later reflection-aware NeRF work adds traced reflection rays because expensive direct neural radiance queries and consistent nearby reflections remain difficult. These are extensions beyond the original c(x,d) parameterization. assertions.source_quote: Multiscale viewing is another unresolved property of the original point-ray formulation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and point-like 5D coordinates. Mip-NeRF reports that this can yield blur or aliasing when training and testing images observe content at different scales; simply casting more rays is expensive because every extra ray multiplies MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical frustums and integrated positional encoding reduce aliasing in that paper, while Mip-VoG later pursues explicit multiscale grids for real-time anti-aliasing. Thus, the foundational renderer integrates a ray but does not itself prefilter the spatial footprint of a pixel. assertions.source_quote: Finally, architectural acceleration introduces its own trade-offs rather than a single universal solution. PVD describes plain MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and their compositions as competing NeRF structures with distinct trade-offs; it specifically notes that hash-table representations train and render faster but lack clear geometric meaning for spatial-relation-aware editing. Hyb-NeRF similarly combines encodings to balance speed, quality, aliasing, and memory. The open problem is therefore not merely making NeRF faster: practitioners must jointly choose representation interpretability, storage, rendering hardware, multiscale behavior, editability, and view-synthesis fidelity.
